body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Landing a table at one of New York City’s buzziest restaurants may now require more than quick reflexes and a carefully timed Resy alert.

	DoorDash has expanded its in-app restaurant reservation service to New York, giving diners another way to book tables at coveted spots including The Corner Store, The Eighty-Six, Dante, L’Artusi, Roscioli, Scarpetta and Tokyo Record Bar. While customers can browse participating restaurants through the DoorDash app, the platform’s exclusive tables and some of its most desirable time slots are available only to DashPass members.
	

	DashPass is DoorDash’s paid membership program, priced at $9.99 per month. Its core benefits include $0 delivery fees and reduced service fees on eligible orders, plus 5% back in DoorDash credits on qualifying pickup purchases and select member-only promotions. DoorDash also offers discounted Lyft rides.


	Among the restaurants leaning into the platform are The Corner Store, Taylor Swift’s favorite Soho hotspot known for its Wagyu French dip, and The Eighty-Six, a West Village steakhouse located in the former Chumley’s space. Both restaurants are exclusively bookable through DoorDash. Other participating destinations range from the Italian favorite L’Artusi to the vinyl-driven omakase experience at Tokyo Record Bar.

	DoorDash also rewards diners for showing up. At launch, standard customers earned $10 in DoorDash credit after completing an eligible reservation, while DashPass members received $12. The credits can be applied to future delivery or grocery orders, although the promotion is subject to availability and may change.
	

	The reservation rollout represents DoorDash’s latest attempt to become a more comprehensive dining platform rather than simply a delivery service. The company moved deeper into the restaurant-booking business after acquiring hospitality technology company SevenRooms for approximately $1.2 billion in 2025. DoorDash Reservations first debuted in Miami before expanding to New York and additional markets.

	Sign up for Dashpass here.

schema.headline: You Can Now Land New York’s Hardest Restaurant Reservations Through DoorDash

title: Dermot Mulroney Leaving ‘Chicago Fire’ in Season 15
description:
Dermot Mulroney is leaving “Chicago Fire” in Season 15, Variety has confirmed.

	The actor, who joined the NBC drama in Season 13 as Chief Dom Pasca
body:
Dermot Mulroney is leaving “Chicago Fire” in Season 15, Variety has confirmed.

	The actor, who joined the NBC drama in Season 13 as Chief Dom Pascal, will wrap up his storyline early in the show’s upcoming season, which premieres on Oct. 7 at 9 p.m. ET.

	Mulroney took a short hiatus from the program in Season 14 before reappearing in the season finale, which ended on a major cliffhanger. In the last episode, Chief Pascal was discussing the future with Severide (Taylor Kinney) when an emergency call interrupts their conversation and sends the squad to a burning warehouse. As several firefighters rush into the building, the roof begins to collapse. While Pascal stayed outside of the fire, it’s unclear if all of the characters will make it out alive.
	

	Mulroney’s impending exit follows the news earlier this week that Joe Miñoso, an original “Chicago Fire” cast member who has played firefighter Joe Cruz across 14 seasons, will also be departing the show sometime in Season 15.


	The new season will also welcome a new showrunner, Victor Teran, who replaces Andrea Newman after 14 seasons. Plus, “BMF” star Da’Vinchi is joining “Chicago Fire” as a new firefighter at Firehouse 51.

	Mulroney is best known for his roles in “My Best Friend’s Wedding,” “The Wedding Date” and “August: Osage County.” He also stars in the Netflix drama “The Hunting Wives.”

	“Chicago Fire” returns on Oct. 7, sandwiched between its “One Chicago” sibling shows “Chicago Med” (starting Season 12) and “Chicago P.D.” (Season 14).

	Deadline broke the news.

schema.headline: Dermot Mulroney Leaving ‘Chicago Fire’ in Season 15

title: Colson Whitehead’s ‘Harlem’ Trilogy TV Show in Development at Apple (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Apple TV has acquired the rights to Colson Whitehead‘s “Harlem” trilogy, Variety has learned.

	The studio is in early development on an ongoing ser
body:
Apple TV has acquired the rights to Colson Whitehead‘s “Harlem” trilogy, Variety has learned.

	The studio is in early development on an ongoing series based on the bestselling crime novels. The material includes 2021’s “Harlem Shuffle,” 2023’s “Crook Manifesto” and the recently published “Cool Machine,” which hit shelves on July 21 and made it onto Barack Obama’s summer reading list.


	Graham Yost (“Silo”) and Aric Avelino (“American Gun”) are adapting the books for the small screen, executive producing alongside Barry Jenkins (director of “Moonlight,” “Mufasa”), Adele Romanski (“Sorry, Baby”) and Mark Ceryak (“Aftersun”) of Pastel; Melissa Bernstein (“Breaking Bad”) of Special Interests; and Whitehead. 
	

	Whitehead’s “Harlem” trilogy is set in New York and spans the 1950s through the 1980s. Blending crime fiction with social satire, the series follows Ray Carney, a furniture salesman who can’t help but be drawn into the criminal underworld of Harlem. The first book, “Harlem Shuffle,” follows Carney in the 1950s and early ’60s as the neighborhood itself undergoes major economic and cultural changes. The second installment, “Crook Manifesto,” is set against the backdrop of riots and the rise of blaxploitation culture, tracking Carney’s increasingly complicated moral compromises through the 1960s and ’70s. And “Cool Machine” follows Carney’s story into the 1980s.

	Whitehead’s work is no stranger to screen adaptation. His novel “The Underground Railroad” was made into a 2021 miniseries by Jenkins for Amazon Prime Video. And his 2019 book “The Nickel Boys” inspired the 2024 film directed by RaMell Ross, which was Oscar-nominated for best picture and best adapted screenplay. Both novels won the Pulitzer Prize. Whitehead’s other books include the post-apocalyptic zombie novel “Zone One” and the modern reimagining of a Black folk hero “John Henry Days.”
	

	Whitehead is repped by CAA and Aragi, Inc.

schema.headline: Colson Whitehead’s ‘Harlem’ Trilogy TV Show in Development at Apple (EXCLUSIVE)

title: DC and HBO’s ‘Booster Gold’ Show ‘Won’t Be Moving Forward,’ Says Writer David Jenkins
description:
DC Studios and HBO’s “Booster Gold” TV series “won’t be moving forward,” writer David Jenkins said on Friday.c

	“My ‘Booster Gold’ won’t be moving
body:
DC Studios and HBO’s “Booster Gold” TV series “won’t be moving forward,” writer David Jenkins said on Friday.c

	“My ‘Booster Gold’ won’t be moving forward,” Jenkins wrote on Threads. “Can’t improve on Mahershala’s lovely statement so I’ll just apply it here as well.” He reposted a quote from Mahershala Ali’s recent GQ profile story in which the actor said he’s moving on from Marvel’s “Blade” movie after it had been announced in 2019 but never went into production.
	

	Jenkins’ statement on “Booster Gold” quoted this post, seemingly drawing a parallel between the stalled productions: “Mahershala Ali officially confirms that he’s moved on from Marvel’s ‘Blade’: ‘For whatever reason, that project is not for me. If they wanted to do it, we would’ve done it. So I have to move on, and I have moved on. Again, you had me under contract, they have billions of dollars, if they wanted to do the movie, we would’ve done the movie. I feel ready to move on from the ‘Blade’ questions. Those questions are for them. They didn’t want to do it, so they should answer that question.'”


	The “Booster Gold” show was announced in 2023 as part of DC Studios’ initial slate reveal for the rebooted universe by James Gunn and Peter Safran. Among those announcements were the “Superman” and “Supergirl” movies, which have both released in theaters, 2028’s “The Batman: Part II,” plus 2024’s “Creature Commandos” series and the “Lanterns” HBO show, which debuts next month. Other projects that were announced to be in the works were Andy Muschietti’s Batman movie titled “The Brave and the Bold,” James Mangold’s “Swamp Thing” movie, an Amanda Waller TV series and a Wonder Woman show called “Paradise Lost.” There was also a movie based on the Authority superhero team, which is no longer in development. DC Studios did not reply to Variety’s request for comment.
	

	Jenkins, who created HBO’s “Our Flag Means Death” pirate comedy, was hired in July 2025 to pen the pilot and serve as showrunner if it was ordered to series. This past April, Gunn had said that “The Authority” was no longer in the works, but added that “Booster Gold” remained in development and “Paradise Lost” was in “extreme development.”

	Booster Gold is a time-traveling hero from the future who goes back in time to the present and pretends to be a celebrity. He’s known for his cocky attitude, teaming up with fellow hero Blue Beetle and traveling with his robot companion Skeets. Booster Gold has appeared as a supporting character in several animated DC shows, but he’s yet to headline a live-action series.

schema.headline: DC and HBO’s ‘Booster Gold’ Show ‘Won’t Be Moving Forward,’ Says Writer David Jenkins

title: Emmanuel Macron to Host Ted Sarandos, Donna Langley, Dana Walden and Pierre-Antoine Capton Among Global Film Leaders at Lumière Summit (EXCLUSIVE)
description: French President Emmanuel Macron will bring together some of the world’s most powerful entertainment executives in the medieval hilltop village of S
body:
French President Emmanuel Macron will bring together some of the world’s most powerful entertainment executives in the medieval hilltop village of Saint-Paul-de-Vence on Sept. 7 for the Lumière Summit, a landmark international event where AI, theatrical exhibition, film financing and the future of independent cinema will be debated. 

	Co-chaired by Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, the one-day summit is expected to bring together CEOs of major global companies, filmmakers, talent, policymakers, exhibitors, figures from the arthouse world, as well as film education advocates.
	

	Among those confirmed to attend are Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos; Donna Langley, Chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment; President and Chief Creative Officer of The Walt Disney Company Dana Walden; Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group Chairman and CEO Tom Rothman; CAA co-chairman Bryan Lourd; WME partner Richard Weitz; Letterboxd CEO Matthew Buchanan; investment executive Daniel Katz; Canal+ Group CEO Maxime Saada; Mediawan co-founder Pierre-Antoine Capton; Pathé president Ardavan Safaee; Cannes Film Festival chief Thierry Frémaux; TF1 CEO Rodolphe Belmer; Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuña; Cinépolis CEO Alejandro Ramírez Magaña; Vue International founder and CEO Tim Richards; and Toho Cinemas president Hiro Matsuoka. Other confirmed participants include the deans of leading U.S. film schools, including UCLA and USC.


	It will be the first time in a century that France hosts a global conference bringing together governments and senior leaders from across the film industry. The last comparable event took place in Paris in 1926, when 435 delegates from 31 countries, including official representatives from 16 governments, gathered to discuss the future of cinema at a pivotal moment marked by the arrival of talking pictures and the rapid rise of Hollywood’s studio system. A century later, the industry finds itself at a moment of profound technological upheaval, this time driven by AI, streaming and the creator economy. As in 1926, some concrete plans will be unveiled during the summit, including the creation of an international NGO dedicated to protecting and promoting independent cinema worldwide, Variety has learned.
	

	Rather than framing the conversation around the traditional rivalry between Hollywood studios, broadcasters and streaming platforms, the summit – which is organized by France’s National Center for Cinema (CNC) which is led by Gaetan Bruel, under the authority of the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs — will look to redefine how governments and industry leaders can work together to preserve the economic, cultural and democratic value of film, television and gaming in an era increasingly shaped by social media and fragmented audiences. Themes that will be discussed include AI, the creator economy, theatrical exclusivity, new financing models, discoverability, public support, piracy, independent cinema, workforce standards, gender equality, sustainability, film preservation and image education.The event marks the latest step in Macron’s efforts to position France as a global power for the creative industries. The idea is said to have emerged after last year’s Choose France investment summit, where Macron met with Sarandos and other senior film executives. Those conversations reinforced his conviction that political leaders need a direct dialogue with the entertainment industry. It also helped spur a crucial reform of France’s tax rebate for international productions that now includes below-the-line costs.

	The Lumière summit also builds on Macron’s broader push to develop France’s creative economy during his presidency, whose second mandate ends next year. Through the France 2030 investment plan, his government has invested €350 million to strengthen film and television production, build studios and ultimately attract big international shoots, such as “The White Lotus” Season 4 and “Emily in Paris.”

	Alongside boasting Europe’s largest theatrical box office market, the country is now home to some of world’s biggest independent media consolidators, including Banijay, which recently acquired All3Media, and Mediawan, which recently completed its merger with North Road and is reportedly eyeing Lionsgate. 

	Last month, France was also named Creative Country of the Year at the 2026 Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity, underscoring the country’s growing influence across the global creative industries.

	Speaking at Cannes Lions in June, Macron previewed the Lumière Summit, calling it “a perfect rendez-vous” for French creativity. “It will be an opportunity to celebrate with our South Korean friends the richness of the cinematographic creation of our two countries, and it will be a perfect rendez-vous for this French creativity,” Macron said. “You will see, beyond what you already recognized and celebrated through this award, that we can go further and be even more creative.”
	

	France has indeed ranked as Europe’s leading destination for foreign investment for seven consecutive years, while this year’s Choose France summit secured €93 billion in pledged investments, particularly in AI and data infrastructure.

schema.headline: Emmanuel Macron to Host Ted Sarandos, Donna Langley, Dana Walden and Pierre-Antoine Capton Among Global Film Leaders at Lumière Summit (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Variety Promotes Matt Donnelly to Executive Editor of Film
description:
Variety has named award-winning investigative journalist Matt Donnelly as Executive Editor of Film.

	In his new role, Donnelly will oversee all of
body:
Variety has named award-winning investigative journalist Matt Donnelly as Executive Editor of Film.

	In his new role, Donnelly will oversee all of Variety’s film coverage in the esteemed print weekly magazine and online website. He will drive breaking news coverage, analysis, investigative reporting, stories from the film festival circuit and chronicles of Hollywood culture.

	Based in Los Angeles, Donnelly assumes the position on August 17. His predecessor, Brent Lang, will be leaving Variety to become editor-in-chief of IndieWire. 
	

	Variety hired Donnelly in 2018 as a senior film writer. He has interviewed many of the most powerful people in Hollywood, and written cover stories on Ted Sarandos, Nicole Kidman, Leonardo DiCaprio, Demi Moore and Meghan Markle. 

	“As a journalist with an unmistakable voice and vision, Matt Donnelly has proven to be one of the toughest — and most fun — reporters covering Hollywood,” said Ramin Setoodeh and Cynthia Littleton, the co-editors-in-chief of Variety. “His deep sources, extensive Rolodex and expansive knowledge of the industry makes him the perfect leader to oversee our film coverage. We also want to congratulate Brent and thank him on his incredible 12 years at Variety. We will miss publishing his byline and working with him on all his extraordinary stories.” 

	“Variety has changed the trajectory of my career in the most meaningful ways,” Donnelly said. “It’s an honor to continue this 121-year tradition of excellence. I am dedicated to maintaining and raising the high bar set by my editor and friend, Brent Lang, and our leaders Ramin Setoodeh, Dea Lawrence and Cynthia Littleton.”
	

	From deeply sourced business pieces to revelatory celebrity profiles, Donnelly has delivered some of the most compelling entertainment business news of the past decade – covering the downfall of Ellen DeGeneres and the implosion of “America’s Got Talent,” to the shuttering of activist studio Participant Media and career film and TV producers banding together to survive in the streaming economy. 

	Donnelly holds a journalism degree from Philadelphia’s Temple University, and previously held positions at the Los Angeles Times, TheWrap, Yahoo and the New York Post. He lives in Hollywood with his screenwriter partner, Donny Sheldon, and his muse, their dog Chester.

schema.headline: Variety Promotes Matt Donnelly to Executive Editor of Film

title: Paramount Seeks Antitrust Trial in November, While States Ask for April 2027
description: Paramount Skydance asked a judge on Friday to schedule its upcoming antitrust trial in November, while a coalition of states and the Writers Guild o
body:
Paramount Skydance asked a judge on Friday to schedule its upcoming antitrust trial in November, while a coalition of states and the Writers Guild of America asked for a date in April 2027.

	The scheduling matters a lot to Paramount, which will begin paying Warner Bros. shareholders $7 million a day on Sept. 30 until the deal is complete. In the filing, Paramount argued that a delay also “prejudices the creative industry, the individuals who work within it, and the consumers who benefit from it.”
	

	The 12-state coalition, including California and New York, filed suit on July 13, alleging that the $111 billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. will unlawfully reduce competition in the basic cable and theatrical distribution markets. The Writers Guild of America filed a separate suit the next day, arguing that it will also harm the marketplace for writers. Paramount has argued that the deal will help consumers by providing a more robust competitor to streaming giants like Netflix and Amazon Prime.


	In the joint filing on Friday, the states asked Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin to schedule a 12-15 day trial starting on April 5, 2027. The Writers Guild of America concurred with the states’ scheduling request.  Paramount wants a 12-day trial beginning on Nov. 4, arguing that any postponement prolongs an uncertain environment.

	“Deciding what projects to commit to, and when, is already difficult for creative professionals tryingto find the right opportunities in a dynamic industry; doing so in an atmosphere of intense businessuncertainty is even harder,” the company’s lawyers argued. 
	

	The states, meanwhile, are seeking additional time to obtain documents and take depositions from Paramount executives. The trial will be held in federal court in Oakland, and will depend heavily on expert testimony from economists.

	In the filing, the states argued that Paramount’s proposed scheduled is rushed and unworkable.

	“Defendants’ proposed schedule would deprive Plaintiff States and the Court of a thorough evidentiary record,” the states argued, saying it would allow for less than two months of fact discovery and one month of expert discovery. “Their extraordinarily truncated schedule unfairly favors Defendants because they (1) have information Plaintiff States need to prove their case and (2) do not bear the burden of persuasion.”

	Paramount faces a deadline to close the deal by June 4, 2027. The WGA argued that such a self-imposed deadline should not dictate the trial schedule.

	Martinez-Olguin granted a temporary restraining order earlier this month that blocked the deal from closing for 28 days. The states were expected to file for a preliminary injunction last week, but in a surprise move, Paramount agreed to put the deal on hold until trial, essentially conceding that an injunction was imminent.

	The state case has presented an unexpected obstacle to the deal, which received approval from the Department of Justice in June. The European Commission and regulators in Australia, China, and many other countries have also signed off on the merger.

	“We believe a trial on the merits is the best and most direct way for us to prove what we’ve said from the start — this transaction is lawful, pro-competitive, and raises no antitrust concerns,” a Paramount spokesperson said, calling the states’ request a “stonewalling tactic.” “Our request for a November trial date is more than sufficient to give both sides the time they need to conduct discovery, gather evidence, and prepare for trial.”

	Attorney General Rob Bonta issued his own statement defending the scheduling request.

	“Our challenge to the unlawful Warner Bros./Paramount merger is a clean-cut antitrust challenge through and through: it’s about protecting the vibrancy of an industry, the pockets of consumers, and the quality of films and television programs that take center stage in many of our lives,” Bonta said. “This challenge deserves careful and thorough review and today my office and attorneys general across the country asked the court for a trial date next spring. We are eager to continue to make our case and look forward to a final determination of the schedule by the court.”

schema.headline: Paramount Seeks Antitrust Trial in November, While States Ask for April 2027

title: As ‘Civilization’ Turns 35, Creator Sid Meier and Firaxis President Look Ahead to a New Ages for 2K Studio’s Franchises
description: Sid Meier‘s four-year-old grandson has a new favorite song and it’s one that is near and dear to fans of the legendary video game developer’s “Civil
body:
Sid Meier‘s four-year-old grandson has a new favorite song and it’s one that is near and dear to fans of the legendary video game developer’s “Civilization” franchise.

	“He is singing ‘Baba Yetu’ day and night. It’s like insane,” Meier tells Variety, noting the preschooler hasn’t actually played the turn-based strategy his grandfather is famous for, but is very familiar with its theme song. “I’m getting these videos of him singing ‘Baba Yetu’ along with the recording.”
	

	While obviously a personal anecdote, Meier says it’s not far from what he’s heard from “Civ” players about how they are now interacting with the Firaxis-developed franchise more than three decades after the initial game’s release. 


	“What I’ve seen more recently is this intergenerational connection,” Meier says. “I’ll talk to a parent and they’ll say, I introduced my daughter or son to ‘Civ,’ and now we play together, and now they want to play. And it’s a community and we listen to them. We update the game with their ideas. We listen to their feedback. We expand the game as time goes on.”



	

	



	“Civilization” is coming up on its 35th anniversary this September, just a few months after the Meier-founded video game studio, 2K’s Firaxis, celebrated its 30th birthday. And for a midsized developer, that’s quite an impressive run, especially given the fact it has remained largely focused on turned-based strategy games, including “Civilization” and “XCOM.”

	“We’re kind of established in a way that many companies are not, and that’s a responsibility,” Meier says. “But that’s a wonderful place to be where people will say, yeah, I’ll take a look at that next game because I’ve enjoyed some of your games in the past. So what’s a little bit unique about Firaxis is the longevity of the company. The 30 years that we talk about — some people have been playing our games for 30 years, and that’s a real gift that we get to take advantage of.’”
	

	Firaxis president and studio head Heather Hazen, who joined the company nearly six years ago, says the developer is in a unique position in a very crowded gaming industry, as it is often its own competition.

	“The benefit that we have in the ‘Civilization’ ecosystem is that ‘Civ 6’ is the biggest competitor to ‘Civ 7.’ And it’s funny because you’re like, ‘Wow, is that a benefit? Is that a tough situation to be in?’ And the truth is, we want our fans to be playing ‘Civilization,’ regardless of which installment it is,” Hazen says. “So we do think about ‘Civilization’ as an ecosystem. How can you play ‘Civ’ when you have 30 minutes versus 30 hours?”

	This leads the Firaxis team to the question they faced just a few years ago when they were coming off “Civilization 6” and preparing to launch “Civilization 7,” which debuted in 2025.

	“We talk about those things a lot: when do we divest or stop working on a ‘Civ’ game? The answer to that is, whenever our fans tell us they want something else,” Hazen says. “We still have people that say ‘Civ 5’ is their favorite game and are installing that game, and ‘Civ 6’ is their favorite and installing that game. So I think we need to do a better job as game developers to make it easy for our fans to transition between their favorite ‘Civ’ experience. And we haven’t quite nailed that ecosystem effect yet, but it’s a thing that we talk a lot about.”

	Meier says the rule of thumb for when Firaxis decides to make a new version of “Civ” is “each iteration had something interesting that really justified it being the next version.”



	

	



	“There are usually 5-6-7-year intervals where we build upon the current game with additional civilizations and leaders and different ways of playing in scenarios and all that kind of stuff,” Meier says. “So there’s a cadence, but it’s a cadence that has a certain logic to it.”

	Firaxis recently launched, “Test of Time,” a major update to “Civilization 7″ following some negative fan feedback about new features included when the game came out last year, including its “Ages” system. And Firaxis made sure this new “Civ 7” update only came out after three rounds of public play testing with fans to get it right.

	“The Ages system was controversial, and so we wanted to hear from fans about what was or wasn’t working in that system, and how we might adapt it to really deliver that sense of continuity and agency that players were used to in ‘Civ,’” Hazen says. “And I think we struck a really great balance with the changes that we made to Ages through the ‘Test of Time’ update.”
	

	Meier says the “Civilization” team has been used to pivoting game features since before the original debuted in 1991. That project started out as a very different title than the turned-based strategy game fans know today. In fact, it wasn’t turn-based when Meier, who had at that time just released “Railroad Tycoon,” first started on the concept with design partner Bruce Shelley.

	“One of the ironies is ‘Civ’ is now known as a classic turn-based game,” Meier says. “The original prototype was not turn-based; it was much more ‘SimCity’-ish, where you would zone areas. In this country, I wanted to be agriculture, and then you’d watch that happen. And then you go over here in this country, maybe they’re into production. It was very much hands off the way ‘SimCity’ is; you watch things. But about halfway through, we made the change to turn-based and actually moving things around and having to really pay attention to what you’re doing, and all of a sudden, your brain is totally engaged in terms of, what should I do next? What’s going to happen if I do this? And that really clicked, that whole idea of turn-based where you get to make all the important decisions and you have plenty of time.”

	Upon the game’s release, the turn-based style went over great — but the initial lineup of 14 playable civilizations, including the Americans, Aztecs and Babylonians, left much to be desired by the rest of the world’s players.

	“When we first made ‘Civ,’ we had no idea how seriously people would take it,” Meier says. “I mean, we got letters from Canadians like, ‘Why aren’t the Canadians in the game? Canadians are just as important as these people.’ And it’s like, oh, we weren’t trying to you define all the rubrics of history, this was just supposed to be a fun game. But we did gradually realize over time that there was this educational aspect of it, where people were learning about countries, about leaders, about history, and we needed to be a little more responsible about how we how we approached that. And there were communities that were underserved and countries that weren’t in the game that should be in the game, and there were concepts that weren’t in the game that we needed to add.”

	For that, Meier says “mea culpa.”

	“We made the original game in a year with three people, so there’s only so much we can do then,” Meier says. “But as the game has progressed, we’ve had the resources to add additional civilizations. And ‘Civ 7’ has done a lot with the Shawnee civilization, for example, and adding different leaders and a lot more diversity and inclusivity with all the different things that we can do now. Also, in terms of gameplay, the original was a little bit tilted toward the military, but now you can be peaceful, you can be scientific, you can be cultural, you can follow different paths. So, part of it is trying to be a little more responsible about the messages that the game gives you, and also be more inclusive. But I will say that global warming was part of the original ‘Civ 1,’ and I’m pretty proud of that.”
	

	The “Civilization” and “XCOM” franchises remain the core of Firaxis’ business, but Hazen says the team is continuing to grow along with those IPs and figure out what they will become over the next 30 years.

	“I think every game studio is going through an evolution now, especially given what we’ve seen happening industrywide over the last several years,” Hazen says. “And to have a studio that has a franchise like ‘Civ’ and a franchise like ‘XCOM’ to be able to build upon and continue to grow is just such an awesome opportunity for any studio. To be in a place where you’ve got 30 years of legacy that is the backbone of where you’re going for the future feels more stable than I’ve had the pleasure of experiencing in my 20-some-plus years in game development.”

	And what the future looks like is uncertain, even to the “Civilization” builder himself.

	“When I finished ‘Civ 1,’ as it’s now known, I thought it was done. I don’t have any more ideas. I put them all in this game,” Meier says. “And what’s been true over the years is each ‘Civ’ game has been really led by a different designer. Because once you do a ‘Civ’ game, your brain is fried and you’ve done everything you can. So I finished ‘Civ 1,’ and I thought, that’s good!”

	Meier’s next project was the 1994 music-generating game “C.P.U. Bach.” 

	“I wanted nothing to do with strategy, I wanted to do a music game — but then [‘Civilization 2’ designer] Brian Reynolds came along and said, ‘I’ve got these ideas for a new “Civ” game. It should be done in Windows,’” Meier says. “Wow, this Windows thing — you can actually change the size of the screen. OK, Brian, you go. And [he said], ‘I think it should be moddable.’ Moddable? Wait a minute, my game is perfect. There’s no reason to do a mod. He was right, and I was wrong. But that whole question of what does the next ‘Civ’ look like is a very interesting one.”

	What Meier does know about “Civilization 8″ is it should follow Firaxis’ internal “one-third, one-third, one-third” rule that they’ve used to make the franchise’s many sequels so far.

	“It should be one-third just a classic mechanic, one-third improved versions of the things that we did last time, and one-third new stuff,” Meier says. “That’s kind of guided how we go from iteration to iteration. Once that one-third new bucket is filled up, we’ve got some good ideas that we’d like to try that we can’t really fit into the current version. So it might be time to do the next version. And each one has had some interesting worthwhile; upgrades or changes that have intrigued people. At one point, we went from squares to hexes. It doesn’t sound that exciting, but it was really really interesting.”

schema.headline: As ‘Civilization’ Turns 35, Creator Sid Meier and Firaxis President Look Ahead to a New Ages for 2K Studio’s Franchises

title: Jon Bernthal on His ‘Brotherly Dynamic’ With Tom Holland in ‘Spider-Man’ and ‘The Odyssey,’ and Why Punisher Is Peter Parker’s ‘Cautionary Tale’

	In 2015, on the set of the peri
body:
Jon Bernthal and Tom Holland‘s superhero trajectory is so intertwined, it could make its own comic book storyline.

	In 2015, on the set of the period drama “Pilgrimage,” Bernthal and Holland filmed each other’s audition tapes for their Marvel roles as the Punisher and Spider-Man, respectively. Now, after playing the parts for a decade, they share the screen for the first time in “Brand New Day.” And the Sony/Marvel movie, which is now playing in theaters, is their second project together in as many weeks, following Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey.”
	

	“It’s great to be able to do two in a row with my friend Tom,” Bernthal tells Variety. “It’s just so beautiful to come full circle.”


	Bernthal took Variety’s call while he raced to the airport to finally head back to the west coast after a long tenure in NYC, where he’d starred in “Dog Day Afternoon” on Broadway, then did back-to-back press tours for “The Odyssey” — where he’d waxed poetic on his character Menelaus’ counsel of Holland’s Telemachus — and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” — where Frank “The Punisher” Castle becomes Peter Parker’s unlikey confidant, using his life as cautionary tale.

	Lately, life has been blissfully busy for Bernthal: the past few months also saw him star in the massively successful Netflix limited series “His and Hers” opposite Tessa Thompson; headline the Disney+ special “The Punisher: One Last Kill,” which he co-wrote with director Reinaldo Marcus Greeen; and wrap up his Emmy-winning role on FX’s “The Bear,” with a special episode written by him and Ebon Moss-Bachrach titled “Gary.”
	

	“Beyond anything, I’m just enormously grateful,” Bernthal says. “To be in New York for this time and doing this play on Broadway, I was very much in touch with that 18-year-old kid who had this dream, that at times seemed sort of impossible and far away,” he continues, referring to his younger self. “I really wanted to honor that kid by doing that play. And when I look at these other projects that I got to have a real hand in creating and writing myself, I’m just so grateful. It’s been a really magical year.”

	But when Bernthal was revealed to be joining the cast of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” early reports didn’t make too much of the moment.

	Most stories (including mine) suggested that Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner/Hulk would slide into the mentor role that’s been a key dynamic in Tom Holland’s previous “Spider-Man” movies, with everyone from Robert Downey Jr.’s Iron Man/Tony Stark to past Spider-Men Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield playing wise sage to Peter Parker.

	After all, Bruce is one of the original Avengers, and until now, Frank has been relegated to Marvel’s TV output — first in Marvel’s Netflix shows and more recently in “Daredevil: Born Again” and his own standalone special on Disney+. Plus, other Spider-Man characters, like villains Scorpion (Michael Mando) and Tombstone (Marvin Jones III), would also appear.

	But it should’ve been obvious that Frank would become Peter’s confidant in “Brand New Day” – and not just because the anti-hero is a mainstay in the Spider-Man comics. A lot of it comes down to the dynamic between the actors who play them. 

	“Jon and Tom have a rapport that would be very difficult to replicate in any scenario, and when the two of them are on screen, I could watch them banter for half an hour,” says “Brand New Day” director Destin Daniel Cretton. “I would just let them go off script, and so many wonderful moments came out of that that ended up in the final cut.”

	In “Brand New Day,” Bernthal’s Punisher is still the lethal vigilante fans know and love. His backstory is tragic: the former U.S. Marine’s wife and children are murdered by the mob, leaving him aimless and (justifiably) angry at the world. And, as the Punisher, Frank is known to enact particularly brutal, bloody vengeance. How could that darkness fit into the heretofore brightly colored “Spider-Man” universe?
	

	“I was very aware of that and very protective of Frank, and I really want to deliver for the fans and the people that he means so much to,” Bernthal begins. “And look, that was really the question. That was really the issue. How tonally would he fit into this world?”

	Bernthal answers that question below and shares more about his “Spider-Man” experience — including what he thinks is next for the Punisher in the MCU.

	
		Fans are very excited about getting the Punisher on the big screen for “Brand New Day,” but the last time we saw Frank was in the very R-rated Disney+ special, “One Last Kill.” What was it like to make him PG-13 for this movie?	

	I was very clear with Destin: we have to believe that he would be able to walk off the set of “One Last Kill,” and be that same guy walking onto the set of “Brand New Day,” while also honoring that tonally it’s a much different project. I deeply appreciated that Amy Pascal, Destin and Tom Rothman all wanted the exact same thing.

	They all really respected and wanted his version of Frank that I’ve been delivering over the years. A lot of times in this business, when there’s an issue, or a little bit of a conflict or a problem, something you’re trying to figure out, sometimes the answer is to sort of skirt around it, or to avoid it, or to gloss over it, rather than to dive into it and to really explore it. I feel like we really hit it head on.

	My dear friend Colton Hill, who’s a Marine and a Green Beret, who I trained with for years, was on set with me as the Punisher. He was behind the camera every time I was there, and he was so helpful. I was so grateful not only that Destin welcomed that, but he was hungry for it, and they became very good friends. It’s a real testament to the kind of filmmaker Destin is that he really wanted to accomplish both of those things — preserving Frank and blending him into the tone of this film.


	
		I laughed at Peter shooting a web over Frank’s mouth to stop him from swearing. What did you think when you saw that in the script?	

	We really leaned a lot on improvisation and finding things on the day. What was great about this project was that you have all kinds of the bells and whistles — I mean, this is no mystery; this is a huge franchise and the level of artistry and talent is immense and unparalleled — but at the end of the day there’s a real vigor and vitality in going after the truth of the scene on the day. It was not a strange thing on that set for them to stop things and have the actors and Destin explore and rewrite and find things and get closer to the kernel of the scene, or to explore through improvisation. I was really grateful for that, and I was very pleasantly surprised by it. This is a new lens in which we see Frank, but it’s not a different character. It’s going to preserve what people love about him most.




	

					Jon Bernthal as The Punisher in “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.”
									Jay Maidment/Columbia/Sony
	



	
		Let’s talk about how Frank and Peter’s relationship evolves. The movie leans into this idea that, in some ways, Frank is a bit of a cautionary tale for Peter, as he disappears into his work and isolates himself. How did you find that dynamic?	

	Tom and I have known each other for a really long time. We have this natural big brother-little brother dynamic. It’s important to always note that Frank is a guy who’s spiraling and reeling from trauma. He’s not looking for any light at the end of the tunnel. He’s not looking to get out of the darkness. He’s looking to dive right into it, and he’s also quite aware that this is no way to live.

	I’m always interested in characters who build walls around their heart, who reject the outside world. Reject the light. Reject friendship, companionship, love. What I love about those kinds of characters is that’s actually an impossible task for a human being. No matter what wall you build around your heart, there’s got to be little holes for the light to shine through. And Tom’s performance as Spider-Man really is that light.

	It’s very clear to Frank the steps that you know Spider-Man is headed [down]; he’s trying to emulate this kind of darkness and this lone wolf mentality. Frank looks at that clearly as what it is: that’s absolutely no place to live. He doesn’t want to go to the places that [Frank has] gone, and he doesn’t want this guy to go feel the things that he feels. This is not something ever to emulate. He sees himself as a cautionary tale.


	
		You’ve known Tom for more than a decade. What was it like to shoot those scenes for “The Odyssey,” where you also have a bit of a mentor-mentee relationship, and then come onto this set and play a similar dynamic?	

	It’s been truly magical to do two films back-to-back with an old friend. The real magic of this business, the real takeaway, is the people that you get to meet along the way. I got to know Tom as a 17-year-old kid, almost 13 years ago. I’d never seen anything like his drive and determination to get [Spider-Man]. The belief that he had it himself. I loved being a part of that.

	Over the years, to see how he’s grown as a movie star and an international celebrity, but then to be able to walk on set of this thing that he’s had such a hand in building — he’s one of the main creative drivers behind this huge [franchise] — I’m really proud of him. To see him now as a man, to see him in love, to see him so solid, to see him so sturdy, but also to see that the things that I loved about him when I first met him are still totally present. He’s a family-first guy. He’s kind to everybody. He’s patient. He’s courteous. He’s unbelievably hardworking and diligent. I really love him. It was a great experience for me to see how far he’s come and that he’s become this unbelievable man, but to also see that he hasn’t changed.


	
		To your point about people who you’ve gotten to continue this journey with: your “The Bear” co-star Liza Colon-Zayas is also in “Brand New Day.” What was it like to have her as a part of the Spider-Man universe?	

	She’s great and “The Bear” has been such a gift for me. I have so much trust in Chris Storer — he’s singular as a TV creator — so, to come back and have that episode with Liza [Season 3’s “Napkins”], that was such a cool gift. It was great seeing her in London, and I’m really happy that she gets to be part of this.


	
		Speaking of “The Bear,” we have to talk about the surprise episode: “Gary.” As a creative, what has it opened for you to be able to get into the weeds with these characters — from Michael Berzatto in the “Bear” to “Punisher: One Last Kill,” and your upcoming series, “The Bottoms” (in development at FX)?	

	Look, I love it. Being an actor and trying to live as an artist has really saved my life. Beyond my family, it’s the single most important thing to me. I’ve been able to grow and explore things as an actor that I’m just so enormously grateful for, and made me a better father, a better husband, a better friend, a better human. I’m so grateful that I’ve found this other thing that I love. I get such joy from it, such satisfaction.

	I can’t really begin to say how much it says about Chris that he gave us this episode to write. To have a show that’s, one, so successful and two, so deeply personal and sacred to him, but to also to treat it with such confidence and such sturdiness to not only allow but to demand the other creatives who are a part of it to collaborate fully and to bring every inch of themselves and their own creativity and their own ideas to it, think nothing real shows genius in an auteur quite like that. It’s the thing that I find uniform among all the greats that I’ve worked with. They demand collaboration. The best idea wins. They’re not ruled by their egos. Chris is just one of a kind. I’m so grateful for this opportunity for me and my dear friend Ebon to explore these characters deeper. The amount of trust in us is so beautiful, and we really did not want to let him down.


	
		While you were doing all these different jobs, “The Bear” aired its series finale. How did you commemorate the show? And celebrate the Season 4 Emmy nominations?	

	I got to be on stage with Ebon every single night on Broadway while it was slowing down, and I think I actually watched the season even before he did. It’s such an interesting process for me, unlike anything else that I’ve ever done before, because I’m really not there very much. I’m talked about, and I sort of drop in, but first and foremost, I’m a fan.

	Really, it was this gift that came out of absolutely nowhere, and it just continued to open me up and challenge me as an artist and provide these unbelievable opportunities. The thing that I love most is I don’t read the script. I don’t know what’s going to happen. I get to watch with everyone else, in this unique position of lingering behind the scenes and in the hearts and imaginations of the people on screen. I honestly thought that this season was the best season, and it was such a beautiful and bold way to end the show. To celebrate what makes a show like this — real collaboration, real joy, real family, falling down and getting back up. It was just such a beautiful ending, such a beautiful season.


	
		“Brand New Day” is hopefully not going to be the end for Frank Castle. Do you think we’re going to see more R-rated or PG-13 Punisher going forward? Is he going to team up with the Defenders in “Daredevil: Born Again” Season 3? What do you want to see next for him?	

	The great thing about what we get to do is you never know what’s going to come next, and that’s something that I come to really embrace and love and celebrate. I don’t know what the next story is with Frank, but I know it’s out there. I think there’s a little bit of Frank Castle in all of us. It’s been such a gift to be able to explore the darkness that is Frank and his life and his struggle and his mission. I’m really eager and excited to keep going with Frank and to see what’s next. But honestly, I don’t know what that is, and I’m still excited to find out.

title: ‘Big Brother 28’ Contestant Jason Breaks Down That Explosive Tea Party and Not Letting Kamu ‘Bully’ Him: ‘Isn’t It Interesting How the Six People in Power Were So Threatened by a Drag Queen?’
description: “Big Brother 28″ contestant Jason De Puy, also known as Salina EsTitties from two seasons of “RuPaul’s Drag Race,” knew the writing was on the wall
body:
“Big Brother 28″ contestant Jason De Puy, also known as Salina EsTitties from two seasons of “RuPaul’s Drag Race,” knew the writing was on the wall when he lost the blockbuster challenge during Thursday night’s live eviction episode.

	“I was this close, a second away, from tying with Mallory. I knew it was game up for me, so I was in acceptance in that house,” Jason tells Variety the morning after being voted out of the house in a 12-0 landslide. “I’m here, no need to be bitter or upset.”
	

	While Jason fully embraced his queerness on the show, he chose not to tell anyone he was a “Drag Race” veteran. Yet “Survivor” favorites Rick Devens and Dee Valladares, alongside “Big Brother 26″ favorite Angela Murray, made a strong pact as reality TV stars.


	“I think those icons are strategic enough players — smart, cunning and baffling enough players — that they would have used that against me down the line,” Jason says.

	While Jason went on quite the emotional roller coaster in the house, “Big Brother” host Julie Chen Moonves let him know during their exit interview that he was among the top three houseguests voted every week to receive a chance at mystery power.

	“That was just eye-opening,” Jason says. “I’m just so honored and grateful that me being exactly who I am was enough for [America] to like me, even though I thought me being who I am made people hate me.”

	Below, Jason breaks down the explosive tea party that sent shock waves through the house, his reaction to Kamu making waves online for his anti-drag comments (as heard on the live feeds), and what he hopes for the future of “Big Brother” after being the first drag contestant in the show’s history.
	
	
		There was a lot of debate in the house in the days leading up to the eviction about different scenarios, and a potential flip. Why do you think all 12 votes ended up being against you?	

	I call it the six — the icons and [Kamu], Chuck and Haley, they’re the ones running this game completely. They got Drew and Barrett in their pocket, they’re the majority. So I definitely see how voting for me would put a target on their backs, especially if they don’t win power. Who are they going to put up next? It fared better for them to not show their cards in that way, I guess. So I understand.
	
		Drew and Barrett have been trying to play the middle. Will that strategy work out for them in the long run?	

	They’re probably going to have to show their cards, but if they stick with the six, I think they’re in a good position. They just need to win some power down the line or hope that Mallory wins. I would assume that Mallory is the only one who would take a shot at the six unabashedly. She’s made it very clear that she has some targets. That’s what is going to take for any shift in the house to happen, because I don’t see Barrett or Drew shifting that. They’re pretty much set up at least through jury, at this point.

	I’m rooting for Barrett. Ultimately, I think he’s set up in a way that if he wins some power, he can make some moves. He has Mallory in his pocket, which is a good thing because the minute she gets power, that can help Barrett [get rid] of Chuck, Haley and Kamu. If the other side gets power, Barrett can use that to his advantage since he’s playing both sides.
	
		The house has been pretty cleanly divided from the beginning, but all the votes have been landslides.	

	That’s what I really learned in the Rome vote, even myself included. I voted Rome out and I had to for my game. If you don’t show your cards, there’s opportunity and possibility to connect with someone else at that point. But if you make a clear line in the sand, you’re ousted, which is what happened to me at the tea party, what happened to me at the nomination ceremony with Devens. I was constantly put up to get attacked, so I wasn’t afraid to combat them. They’re kind of scaredy cats, they’re afraid to stand up.
	
		You and Kamu clearly did not get along in the house. I’m wondering how much you perceive Kamu’s dislike of you as personal versus game.	

	I could tell that it was personal, but he was using game to make that point. He would call me his “zesty bestie,” and I don’t really know where that came from because we weren’t necessarily besties at all. It felt a little bit like a pet name at first, where I was like, “Oh, he’s trying to relate to me!” But as soon as he ousted me, I learned very quickly — I don’t know what it was, but I could tell it wasn’t authentic. I think you’re more zesty than me, dude! What are you talking about?
	
	
		Frankie Grande, who was on Season 16, is one of your close friends and has been very outspoken online. I don’t know if you’ve had a chance to connect with him yet, but he has posted about some of Kamu’s anti-drag comments.	

	Oh wow, no, I have not talked to Frankie yet. Has he been helping with that conversation out in the real world?
	
		Yes!	

	That’s awesome. I mean, that’s very Frankie. I’ve known Frankie now for about 13 years and watching him live authentically himself, I see the backlash he gets. I see the negativity, the negative comments. People love to clown on him. Although it may hurt, I see how he rises above it by just being himself even more. I think I took a page from his book in that house with Kamu, right? I wasn’t gonna let him bully me, I wasn’t gonna let him make me hide away in the closet. I was gonna battle him, and I was going to step up and be even more authentically myself. And that’s exactly what he got that next morning after the tea party.
	
		Let’s talk about that explosive tea party! You seemed to clock that Kamu didn’t really want to clear the air and was instead trying to air you out, making you look worse.	

	Correct. I could tell that’s what he was doing. I was proud of myself for standing up for myself, that was the most awesome part — the fact that I didn’t let him win with the teapot the next morning. I was gonna make sure he knew who the queen of the house was because he was trying to be the queen of the tea party. Baby, you can’t out queen a drag queen!
	
		What was the inspiration for banging the pots and pans around the house? You took a page from Evel Dick and Josh’s playbook.	

	Honestly, I never thought I would have the balls to do something like that. In a way, I thought, “Oh, that’s such a desperate move to try to get airtime!” But the way things panned out, the way I was cornered, it was so perfectly set up that it was a tea party with a tea kettle available. I was fuming in bed, I could not sleep. Kamu’s words had me so irritated in bed! I was like: “There’s a tea kettle. What happens when a tea kettle gets hot? It whistles!”
	
		Kamu made some comments on the live feeds that were questioning drag performers.	

	I heard something!
	
		He told Devens: “Bro, miss me with the drag stuff … I’m still an MMA guy, and I have an image to uphold.”	

	Awesome! That’s a sentiment across America with a lot of big straight guys, right? The idea of drag queens is very threatening to them. Headlines also help perpetuate that idea. My hope is that by me being the first drag queen in the house, without ever putting a stitch of makeup on, without ever putting on a dress — you know, Drew and Barrett wore a dress, and they’re straight boys! I never paraded that in front of the house, I never paraded that in front of Kamu. I hope just me being my authentic self is an example to America that drag queens are not threatening in a physical, violent way. Even with my words, I thought I was fairly respectful, even though my words could be sassy and cunning. I hope my example of what a drag queen looked like in the house can show America that we’re nothing to be afraid of. Maybe in the “Big Brother” house, you should be afraid and not come for a drag queen! And I hope I made that very clear. But in life, baby, I’m just an artist, I’m a creative who’s trying to make a name and make a living for himself.
	
	
		You had some explosive moments with Angela. What is your reaction to Drew being the one to rat you out about lying and manipulating Angela with your dead mother story?	

	That really surprised me. I thought Angela being a returning player knew to look in the mirror to see if people were being authentic. I really thought that’s how I got ousted, I didn’t know it was Drew until earlier this morning. The next day after I created the Court Jesters’ alliance with Drew and Melody, I had a feeling that they went against me and created an alliance with Rome and Lyric. But apparently, Drew had an alliance with the icons day one.

	Had I lied at the nomination ceremony, maybe that would have made Drew look like  someone to be questioned by Angela and I would have had her. So I should have lied, but it was in my nature in that moment to just own up to it and be honest. And good job, Drew!
	
		So it was the right move for him?	

	I hope it bites him in the butt because sure, you made these big splashes and big moves early on. I think this cast is smart enough to see what’s happening.
	
		Where did you leave things off with Angela?	

	I would love to see her get eliminated just because I want to see her crumble! But I like Angela. I think she really likes me. She really wanted to connect with me so much in the house, but I was not letting her because of the game aspect. She wanted to connect with me on a human level, but not on a game level. We’ll be fine after the show, we’re fine now. We have an understanding, game clocks game.
	
		And why is no one going after the vets? It seems like every season, nobody goes after the returning players.	

	That’s why I didn’t align with them in the beginning. I have that exact sentiment when I watch the show: “Get the vets out!” I told that to Drew, and Drew went to them, and look what happened.
	
		I don’t know if you saw but Haley is HOH now. It seems like things are going to keep moving the same.	

	It’s gonna be boring!
	
		We need a flip!	

	We need a flip. Mallory is the one who’s willing to take the shot. She’s also a little bit of a comp beast, she won her veto, the blockbuster and almost won veto last week. It’s very clear that she’s down to put Dee, Kamu and Haley up not the block. The fact that she wants to target Dee is a big deal.
	
	
		Lastly, as the first drag contestant on the show, what are your hopes for future representation on “Big Brother” and reality TV as a whole?	

	My favorite thing about “Big Brother” is how the cast reflects America in real time, right? Isn’t it interesting how the six people in power were so threatened by a drag queen? We see that headline constantly these past couple years — they’re targeting drag queens, they’re targeting our trans brothers and sisters, our queer rights constantly. My favorite thing is that without ever putting on a wig or a dress, I got to represent what drag looks like in the house with just being myself — the messy, emotional, authentic human that I am. That’s what people are so threatened by. I’m proud of the way that I was never violent, that makes me very happy. I hope I showcased my community in a very beautiful light, even though I was attacked the entire time in the house.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: Utah Pageant Queen Who Died by Suicide at 21 Was in Therapy for Personal Struggles
description:
Utah Pageant Queen
                          Dies by Suicide at 21
                          ...
body:
Utah Pageant Queen
                          Dies by Suicide at 21
                          ... Was in Therapy Personal Struggles
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 31, 2026
                            1:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Utah beauty queen Brynn Carnesecca died by suicide just weeks before she was due at her next pageant ... and it's a shock to those who knew her, because we're told she was seemingly doing well in therapy.
      
    
            A close friend of Brynn tells TMZ ... she had recently been enjoying her therapy and even felt she was "doing a lot better," making her suicide even more surprising. The friend tells us they knew about her struggles ... but never realized they were that bad.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The companion saw Brynn just a few weeks ago, where they shared laughs and watched the sunset together. The friend describes the journalist and pageant queen as "a light that was so bright" who brought good energy to those around her.
      

            Brynn's friend says she was always concerned for everyone, loved everyone who she was around, and always tried to improve herself.
      
    
            Unfortunately, she died on Sunday ... with her mom, Michele Carnesecca, confirming her suicide to local outlet KSL.
      
    
            Brynn was crowned Miss American Fork in 2024 and earned the Miss Congeniality Award at Miss Utah in 2025. She was scheduled to compete at the Miss Provo pageant competition on August 22.
      
    
            She also founded Envelopes of Hope, which fostered pen pal relationships between locals in Fork and inmates.
      
    
            She was just 21.
      
    
            RIP

title: Luigi Mangione Pissed At Prosecutors, Wants His State Trial Broadcasted Live
description:

body:
Luigi Mangione
                          STATE PROSECUTORS TRYING TO SCREW ME OUT OF LIVE TV TRIAL
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 31, 2026
                            1:35 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Luigi Mangione is not happy with prosecutors in his state trial ... he says they're doing too much to limit the number of people in court ... and he wants the proceedings broadcast live on air.
      
    
            Luigi's lawyers sent a letter to Judge Carro on Friday ... and it's clear Luigi is mad that the state plans to partially exclude the public and the press from his trial.
      
    
            According to the letter, Luigi has a big issue with the fact that the court and the District Attorney plan to hand-pick the reporters who are allowed to attend the trial.
      

            He's also pissed that the court isn't planning to broadcast his trial to an overflow courthouse ... and that he wasn't "provided with the right to be heard" before these decisions were made.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            Luigi says these things violate his constitutional rights -- specifically under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments -- and is asking for his trial to be broadcast live, just like his arraignment.
      
    
            It seems the court wants to keep things small ... but Luigi wants as many eyes on him as possible as he stands trial for allegedly murdering UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

            Chrisean Rock swears she had nothing to do with ex-boyfriend Karon "Ronny Doe" Cann's murder ... claiming police have ruled her out.
      
    
            Chrisean was streaming when she started distancing herself from the murder investigation ... claiming police already told her, "We know you didn't do it, we got his phone."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She said police interviewed her on camera and recorded her answers ... and she said she welcomed the investigation because she wants to find out who killed Karon.
      

            Chrisean said there were other things at play around the time Karon died that had nothing to do with her, claiming he was on a bunch of substances.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The way Chrisean tells it, no one was holding him accountable, saying ... "Nobody was trying to save Karon before he died." She also alleged people were trafficking drugs through his basement.
      
    
            She also called out trolls for talking about her dead ex, saying they never asked how she was feeling about it.
      
    
            Still, she says she didn't feel much because he was trying to "kill" her by diminishing her character, messing with her image, and "clout chasing" through her son.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Karon was shot and killed in February 2025 ... cops found him with multiple gunshot wounds outside a house in Severn, Maryland. He was taken to a nearby hospital, where he died.
      
    
            Police told us just this week that the investigation is still open and active ... but it's been over a year, and they still haven't publicly identified a suspect or person of interest.
